title: Incremental polynomial-time binary-matroid circuit enumeration
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, for every explicitly given binary matrix \(A\in\mathbb F_2^{r\times m}\), enumerates all circuits of its column matroid exactly once in incremental polynomial time while using space polynomial only in the input length? Equivalently, does binary-matroid circuit enumeration belong to \(\mathrm{IncP}^{\mathrm{poly}}\) under the source’s conventions? The target permits any fixed polynomial exponent in the number of outputs; retaining the known quadratic incremental exponent is a stronger variant distinguished in the later source.
why: This is a concrete test of whether the storage used by saturation-based enumeration is intrinsically necessary. A polynomial-space incremental algorithm would make all minimal binary linear dependencies accessible in output-sensitive time without retaining an exponentially large history, and could suggest methods for other closure-based enumeration problems.
status_note: The checked 2021/2023 habilitation and the author’s WEPA 2022 extended abstract pose polynomial-space incremental enumeration of binary-matroid circuits as open. The July 2026 regularization paper, checked in its publisher introduction and the 2024 author preprint, assumes an already polynomial-space algorithm and does not by itself settle saturation storage. Bounded primary-source searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching algorithm or general lower bound. This is not exhaustive certification of present openness.
review_note: Completed individual review against P versus NP on 2026-09-16; see research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

progress.text: Khachiyan and coauthors give incremental polynomial-time circuit enumeration with independence queries, within a broader family of matroid generation problems.
The habilitation isolates polynomial space for binary-matroid circuit enumeration as Open problem 4.3.
The WEPA extended abstract asks both for polynomial space with the known quadratic incremental bound and, more generally, for membership in polynomial-space IncP.
The journal regularization theorem removes buffering overhead from algorithms that already use polynomial space; its assumptions do not provide the requested compression of saturation storage.

sentences: A circuit of a binary matroid is a nonempty inclusion-minimal linearly dependent set of matrix columns.
The question asks to enumerate all circuits exactly once in incremental polynomial time using memory polynomial only in the matrix input length.
The running time for the first k circuits may be polynomial in k, but the memory bound must remain independent of the number already output.
Incremental enumeration is known with large saturation storage, while polynomial-space regularization assumes that this memory problem has already been solved.
A positive answer would expose all minimal binary dependencies efficiently without storing an exponentially large circuit history.

definitions:
The field \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\) has addition and multiplication modulo two. The input matrix has nonnegative dimensions \(r,m\), represented by unary dimension headers followed by its \(rm\) entries in row order. Its encoded length \(L\) is of order \(r+m+rm+1\), including isolated zero columns and zero-dimensional cases. Malformed encodings are rejected in polynomial time. Column indices are distinct ground-set elements, even if their vectors coincide.

The column matroid has ground set \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). A subset is independent exactly when its columns are linearly independent over \(\mathbb F_2\). A circuit is a nonempty inclusion-minimal dependent subset: \(C\subseteq[m]\) is a circuit if \(\operatorname{rank}(A_C)<|C|\) and every proper subset of \(C\) is independent. Equivalently over this field, the columns in \(C\) sum to zero and no nonempty proper subset has zero sum. A zero column gives a singleton circuit; two equal nonzero columns give a two-element circuit. A circuit is not required to have globally minimum cardinality.

The output for each circuit is its \(m\)-bit characteristic vector. Every circuit must occur once, no other set may be output, the order is unrestricted, and enumeration must halt. Let \(N(A)\) be the number of circuits, which can be exponential in \(L\). If there are no circuits, the algorithm must halt in polynomial time. The output stream is write-only and cannot be read back as free external memory. Registers or buffers retaining previously emitted vectors count toward working space.

Use the source’s deterministic random-access machine convention: finite programs, integer registers, basic arithmetic consisting of addition, subtraction and multiplication, with arithmetic cost proportional to operand bit lengths and unit-cost register access and other basic instructions. Working space counts the bits in all stored integers, including retained outputs and register addresses needed to access them. Output uses designated registers; its polynomial-length encoding may be charged explicitly without changing the class. There is no advice or randomness. The matrix is read-only input and contributes polynomially many bits even if copied into memory.

Incremental polynomial time means that there are fixed positive integers \(C,a,b\) such that, on every valid \(A\) and for every \(1\leq k\leq N(A)\), the time from the start through the \(k\)-th distinct output is at most \(C(L+1)^b(k+1)^a\). Preprocessing is included. Total time through termination is at most \(C(L+1)^b(N(A)+1)^a\), enlarging constants or exponents if necessary. Polynomial working space means that fixed positive integers \(D,c\) bound space at every moment by \(D(L+1)^c\), independently of \(k\) and \(N(A)\). All constants are uniform over matrices and dimensions. These are class-membership bounds, not a prescribed delay exponent or an order requirement.

The cited original circuit-enumeration algorithm also accepts a matroid through an independence oracle. On the promise that the matroid is binary, that representation and an explicit binary matrix are interchangeable with polynomial overhead: greedily find a basis \(B\), make its columns unit vectors, and for every \(e\notin B\) set its coordinate at \(b\in B\) to one exactly when \((B\setminus\{b\})\cup\{e\}\) is independent. In a binary matroid these are the unique fundamental-circuit coordinates and give a representing matrix with at most \(m\) rows. This uses polynomially many queries and polynomial space. Conversely, Gaussian elimination simulates independence queries from a matrix. Oracle queries are exact, and writing their \(m\)-bit sets is charged; the equivalence uses the binary promise and does not apply to arbitrary matroids.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such an algorithm exists, or that no such algorithm exists. A positive proof must establish completeness, absence of duplicate outputs, termination, one uniform incremental polynomial bound and one simultaneous polynomial working-space bound for every binary matrix. A negative proof must rule out all algorithms meeting these bounds, not merely show that the known saturation algorithm stores exponentially many circuits. Polynomial total time without the prefix guarantees, unrestricted output-sized memory, enumeration with repeated circuits, or bounds only for graphic matroids do not settle the target. A conditional lower bound under an unproved complexity assumption is partial progress on this unconditional question.

source_formulation.text: Can the circuits of a binary matroid be enumerated in incremental polynomial time using only polynomial space?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Open problem 4.3; the later WEPA question explicitly separates arbitrary polynomial incremental time from retaining its known quadratic exponent.

context_blocks.text: Circuits are the minimal linear dependencies among columns. Enumerating all subsets and testing rank uses little memory but can waste exponential time before finding early circuits. At the other extreme, storing the whole discovered family can support efficient generation but violates the requested space bound when the family is large.

The known algorithm generates circuits in incremental polynomial time by repeatedly using closure relations among circuits already found. The publisher’s original abstract states the result even for general matroids given by independence queries. The source singles out binary matroids for the additional polynomial-space question.

A zero-sum subset of binary columns need not be a circuit: it may contain several smaller dependencies. Gaussian elimination readily tests whether a proposed subset is a circuit, but this membership test does not by itself provide a way to visit all minimal dependencies with the required output-sensitive time bound.

For graphic matroids, represented by graph incidence matrices over the two-element field, circuits correspond to simple graph cycles. Binary matroids include more than this graphic subclass. An algorithm specialized to graph cycles therefore supplies an example of tractability without settling all binary representations.

Rerunning an enumeration to recognize duplicate outputs can trade additional incremental time for reduced storage when the underlying generator already has polynomial space. It does not automatically remove the large stored family that a saturation generator needs to create its future outputs. This distinction is why eliminating duplicate filters and eliminating the saturation memory are separate tasks.

The later WEPA formulation records a known bound quadratic in the number of generated circuits, times an input polynomial, and asks both whether that exponent can be retained in polynomial space and whether any polynomial incremental exponent can be obtained. This card keeps the latter class-membership target stated by the imported card, while recording the stronger timing question.

The 2026 regularization theorem turns polynomial-space linear incremental algorithms into polynomial-space polynomial-delay algorithms. Its input algorithm must already have polynomial space. Thus it resolves a buffering issue but does not directly compress the circuit family stored by the known saturation procedure. The paper’s black-box lower bounds likewise do not rule out a new algorithm exploiting the matrix.
